en: Continuation of the *Fozu Tongji*, Section One: Biographies of Various Masters—
Dharma Master Fanzhao, Dharma Master Wengao, Dharma Master Zhijue,
Dharma Master Yongqing, Dharma Master Ziyi, Dharma Master Yunze, Dharma Master Yuankai, and Dharma Master Xingcheng.
The Second Part of the Biographies of Various Masters in the Continued *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), compiled by Dharma Master Mengrun, Dharma Master Hongji,
Dharma Master Benwu, Dharma Master Yunruo, and Dharma Master Shanji.
Master Bicai, Master Puyao, Master Zhengshou, Master Zishi, Master Dayou,
Master Huirui, Master Zisi, Master Puyong, Master Zuni, Master Hongdao, Master Youkui, and Master Ruxi.
Compiled by the Dharma Masters Zipeng, Dashan, Liangyu,
Yuanling, and Shaozong;
a continuation of the *Fozu Tongji*, Volume One.
Dharma Master Fazhao, whose courtesy name was Huiryan, was a successor of Dharma Master Fenyin of Beifeng. He was a native of Dadao in Huangyan, Taizhou, belonging to the secular Tong clan.
His lineage had gathered for over four hundred years. His father, Mian, served the Buddha and venerated the monk Bitongfo at Chongsanli; he fathered nine sons, of whom the Master was the eldest.
Next, his mother, Lady Chen, dreamed that the sun pierced through the clouds as she lifted her skirt and conceived him. After twelve months, she gave birth;

his appearance was extraordinary and majestic, with ears reaching down to his shoulders and eyes that sparkled like lightning. Upon entering primary school, his spiritual capacity was already exceptional; he possessed great insight into the Confucian classics.
At the age of thirteen, he followed his father’s aspiration and wished to become a monk; he took ordination under Master Xuan of Shengshui.
One night, he returned from a neighboring temple; the monks saw two brilliant torches approaching and drew near to them, only to find they were his eyes.
Monk Yuexi Hui said to the head seat Kan of Duofu, "This youth is extraordinary; he will surely revitalize our school. Kan performed the tonsure for him.
Thereafter, he studied at Dongye, where he applied himself diligently to the teachings of the Tripitaka and recited the entire canon three times. He then traveled throughout the various regions.
He first went to Beichan to pay his respects to Master Yin of Beifeng. Next, he studied under Master Yan Xiweng of Jiangshan. When Beifeng resided at Xiazhu, he invited the Master to return;
through their discussions and the transmission of teachings, the Master attained clear realization. Upon Beifeng’s passing into *parinirvāṇa*, the Master struck his staff and returned to the east.
Prime Minister Qian built the Hall of Eminent Monks to welcome him. At the age of thirty-three, he left to reside at Yangdan, where he subsequently changed [his name].
He resided at Tiantai Daci. He moved to Shengshui. The Marquis of Shi (Shi Weiwang) appointed him to reside at Yanqing in Yunjian.

He subsequently moved to Fengshan Baqin. The Chancellor, Duke Yong of Shi, appointed him to reside at Siming. The two masters Hai and Shun came from Japan to hear his lectures and requested the *Dujiao ji* (Record of Reading the Teachings) he had composed;
they painted his portrait and returned to their country with it. [The record was also sought by] Chancellor Choe of Goryeo.
He also sent a letter inquiring about the great essentials of the Buddha-dharma and requested a portrait of the nine patriarchs.

Furthermore, he presented the Master with a fine porcelain bowl, a gold inkstone case, and fragrant medicines. When the seat at the Yuyang Monastery became vacant, the local administration invited him to concurrently reside there, but he declined, saying:

"From the Liang and Sui dynasties onwards, Bodhidharma and Zhiyi each had their own lineages of succession. I shall nominate Chijue Chong to take my place. [The official] then seized the temple gardens for the purpose of brewing wine.
The Abbot [Zongxiao] immediately packed his belongings and fled by way of the East Aisle. There, the disciples from both mountains welcomed him at the border.

Lord Bao Hongzhai invited Zhizhe Zhenjue to restore the ancestral temple. Emperor Lizong, having heard of the Master’s reputation, issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Lower Tianzhu, and subsequently transferred him to Upper Tianzhu.
He was appointed as the Right Street Inspector (Jianyi) and specially bestowed the title of Dharma Master Foguang. He was further promoted...

He was appointed as the Supervisor of the Left Street (Zuōjiē). He was granted a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* and summoned to appear before the Emperor at Yìguìgé Hall, where his responses met with imperial approval.

At that time, Jìqìng Temple was completed, and an imperial decree ordered him to serve as its founding abbot (*kāishān*). He declined this earnestly and instead nominated the White Lotus Master Nánfēng Chéng to take his place.

The following year, when Chéng passed away, a special decree promoted him to the position of General Supervisor of the Left and Right Streets (*Zuǒyòu Jiē Dū Sēnglù*), ordering him to concurrently reside at the temple; however, this was not permitted.

He declined the appointment. The Emperor bestowed upon him the two large characters "Huìyán" (Secluded Rock) written by His Imperial Hand. The Master said, "I shall deliver an unimpeded lecture. Students from all three schools—Chan, Teaching (Dharma), and Vinaya—assembled like clouds;
those who heard him attained much understanding and enlightenment. He was summoned to appear at the Yǎnxiàng Hall to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Furthermore, the Emperor wrote "Língshāntáng" (Hall of the Spirit Mountain) in large characters to grant him as a gift. He dispatched his nephew, the Military Counselor Wǔjīngjí Tóngyán, to present the Imperial brushwork.

He returned to his native village. After being summoned for an audience by the Crown Prince, he lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in the Right Hall and was again bestowed with a purple-lacquered robe.

While observing a fast at Minghua Hall, he earnestly petitioned to return to the mountains. When Emperor Duzong ascended the throne, he issued an imperial decree for him to reside once more at Upper Tianzhu.

He remained there for twenty-four years in total. The Chancellor, Duke Jia Wei, commissioned the construction of a stupa for him on the eastern ridge of the temple. [The Emperor] submitted a memorial...
He requested that the Etten Rock Pagoda Temple be granted three *qing* of land to assist with the incense and lamps. That autumn, he manifested illness and moved back to the pagoda temple.
He rejected medicine and dismissed his physicians, composing a text for his own funeral rites. On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he wrote a verse, saying:
"The immortal’s lifespan is eighty years; I have nine more. When empty space is overturned, the Great Function manifests. Having set down his brush, he sat upright and passed away.
He reached the age of eighty-nine and had been a monk for seventy-four years.
He was born on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the *Chunxi* year of the *Yisi* cycle, and passed away on the fifteenth day of the eighth month in the *Xianchun* era.

His senior disciples included Miaosheng, Jixi, Shi, Ju, and over forty others. He personally ordained more than one hundred people. His entire body was enshrined in a tomb, accompanied by his robes and hair.

He was interred at Jintianyan Tomb; this fulfilled his original aspiration. In the following year, he was posthumously granted the title "Ordinary Dharma Master," and his stupa was named "Compassionate Response.

Because of the master’s profound and vast learning, his lofty and penetrating insight, his swift and sharp intellectual acuity, and his expansive capacity for tolerance, he had mastered both Chan and Vinaya without exception.
Regarding the illusory world with equanimity, he was not ensnared by material things; no one could...
Thus, one may gain a glimpse of its limits. His virtue was manifest throughout the monastic community, and his fame spread abroad.

From the Emperor, who held him in high esteem, down to the eminent dukes and great ministers, all wished to associate with him. The teachings of the Hengtai school flourished most greatly under this Master.

There are twenty fascicles of his *Record of Reading the Teachings* (*Du jiao ji*) currently in circulation; other sermons and writings are fully preserved in his separate collection. Such was the Master’s conduct.

The Master’s style was Nanjian. He resided at Lingjiu Peak in India and shared an inseparable friendship with Mr. Tang Wenqing Han, for whom he composed poems and prose in response to the latter's verses.

Furthermore, he requested a gnarled cypress from the Academicians of Wu, saying: "Yesterday, I was honored by your promise to grant me a gnarled cypress; this sufficiently attests to your extraordinary magnanimity.
However, were it not for our worldly bond of friendship, I would not have dared to make such a request. If you would honor your word, please select two [trees]."
When the tree was of a height proportionate to its girth, he bestowed upon it the [name] "The Arrow" (Dik), so that the eyes of the multitude might gaze upward in admiration;
thus the bird’s arrival increased the mountain’s excellence, and the precious gift was not in vain. (And so forth. Chan Master Wuwen Can offered a memorial in verse, saying:

"In the past, when I traveled to Chang’an, I saw you beneath Flying Eagle Peak. Clutching illness and burdened by greed, my carriage was weary and distressed; it was almost as if you had granted me lodging."
He nourished himself among springs and rocks, and found solace within paintings; they came upon him suddenly and departed in an instant.
The Master did not grow weary or weary of them, even after such a long duration. It has now been seventy years since he returned south of the Great River, clad in green *zhú* and blue *qié* robes.
His capacity was like Mount Tai receiving the clouds; his spirit was like the spring breeze touching all things. His dignified bearing and refined demeanor remained vividly before my eyes and mind.

Last autumn, when my elder brother returned to the capital, the Master sent me a letter filled with profound emotion and intense passion, vastly different in tone from the correspondence we had exchanged in the past.
Having read it, I wondered: "Is this old man weary of the world?"
How vast is the interval between worlds! How profound is the distinction of these words! Before long, those who previously harbored doubts came to believe this as true. Alas!
How tragic it is that the oral teachings need not be expounded for the Dharma of the mind to accord with the Sūtras;

that the multitude need not be numerous for their radiant brilliance to surpass that of India and Central Asia; and that wealth need not be accumulated for one’s expenditure to exceed that of Yidun. Heaven and Earth...
How magnificent! How many such individuals can one encounter in a hundred years? I still recall when I sat in attendance upon him;

in his rising and descending, his advancing and retreating, there was not a trace of the ordinary man in his eyes. His resonance was like that of Shukai, his purity like that of Xiaoshan, and his elegance like that of Guanqing.
Harmony is like nurturing the upright; one looks up with reverence and receives impressions with clarity, never having leisure to respond to all at once.

Now these three sons of mine can no longer be found. Xiao Shan has retreated deep into the clouds of the Terrace; Can has become utterly dazed and will likely wither to death amidst the marshes of Jiangnan.
Even the master of the Northern Road can no longer be seen. Gazing afar toward the foot of the North Mountain, I imagine him naturally opening the cave-dwelling and dwelling therein as he pleases.
The Linglong Terrace and pavilions remain as they were; the fresh and bright pines and cassias remain as they were.

Can the people of this age ever again match the prosperity of former times? I do not know on what day he will be gathered [in death], nor at what time he will be buried, nor where his stupa will stand.
Since my old friends in Chang’an have given me no word, and the world is so vast and distant, there is nowhere to whom I may turn for inquiry.
My grief is soundless; my words lack ornament. Amidst the monkeys and cranes of the mountains, my severed soul finds its occasional response.
The Dharma-successor of Master Tongsuan is the Dharma Master named Wengao, style name Ruhui.
His surname is Yu (Yusheng), and his ancestors were from Kaifeng. He was born with the brilliance of the finest talent.
He styled himself "The Ancient Mirror" (*Gujing*), for when his mother was first pregnant, she had been startled awake by the sight of a great round mirror.
Having lost his parents early, the monk Shixun of Qingning Temple told him that leaving the household life would be a way to repay their kindness; the Master followed this advice.

At eighteen, he received full ordination. His nature was pure and simple; he was so conscientious that he never parted from his *uttarāsaṅga* robe. At that time, Master Xin of Zongan was highly esteemed within the Tiantai school.

Master Ying of Tanchan traveled among them, thoroughly investigating their fundamental tenets. One night, he dreamed that the deity Vaiśravaṇa stood upon a multi-storied pavilion holding a pair of arrows;
the Master wished to ascend but was unable to do so. Suddenly, Yuanyan beckoned him from the side, and he climbed up with ease and looked out with clear vision.
All these were ancient scrolls of the Great Teaching; some were transcriptions made by his own hand. Early one morning, he inscribed them upon the walls of the Qǐngníng hermitage.

While residing at Tiānzhú Língshān, he was invited to serve as the First Seat. When Tǎn’ān heard his formal proclamations (*tíchăng*), he sighed and said, "The contents of my alms-bag have now found their successor.
Later, while speaking casually about the matter of the "held arrow," Yuán’ān remarked, "Your spirit has already met with mine."
The worthy sage later resided alternately at the two temples of Upper and Lower Zhu; was this not a portent? In the Wuchen year of the Jiading era, he resided at Guangfu Tasi in Qingzhen.
Several dozen bandits arrived at night carrying weapons; the Master showed no sign of fear and gave them whatever he had stored. He once said:
"If one's study does not lead to awakening, one cannot penetrate the Buddha’s intent; if one's practice is not secret, it will not..."

One is thus able to enter the domain of the sages. For this reason, the duration for various samādhis is often set at seven times seven days and nights; a period of forty-nine days has generally become the standard.
Herein, I cite what resembles the verse of Zong’an: "A pack of fools suffer from madness; for seven times four days and nights, they do not sleep."

Exhausting his mother’s vital energy, he clearly sought heaven by digging the earth. Furthermore, during the relocation of the King of Wu, he visited Jianfu, Yanqing in Yunjian, and Baqin on Fengshan;
it was only at Guangfu that he arrived three times in succession. In the autumn of the Renchen year, an imperial decree appointed him as abbot of Lingyin Temple on Mount Tiantai.
In the third year of the Duanping era, an imperial messenger brought the Emperor’s private casket and bestowed the title "Wuliang" (Immeasurable) upon him.
A statue of the Buddha Amitāyus was enshrined, and a pavilion was constructed to honor it solemnly. The imperial seal (Quízhāng) inscribed its plaque, which shone like the Milky Way.
In the Jiǎhài year, when the seat of Upper Zhū (Shàngzhú) became vacant, Zhao Gùquán, the Dúnmíng of Jīngzhào, memorialized that no one could replace Wén Gǎo; the Emperor’s decree stated, "So be it.
The following year, [Wén Gǎo] appeared to have some internal unease and submitted a petition requesting his retirement. Previously, the laywoman Ló of Xìn had established [the foundation].
The Baohua Monastery was intended for the Master to be its founding patriarch; now that his wish had been fulfilled, the monks of Upper Zhi (Shangzhu) earnestly entreated him to return.
During a drought, the Great Being (Guanyin) appeared at Mingqing Temple. On the final day of the sixth month, the Master entered the palace to offer his thanks.

On the Bingyin day, the Emperor visited the temple to request prayers. The Master’s petition was so sincere and earnest that the Emperor was moved to deep sorrow; as the imperial carriage returned, it rained.
He was immediately appointed as the Monk Registrar (Senglü) of the Left Street, with the mandate to oversee public affairs of the Buddhist teachings, and was granted the title of Dharma Master Fohui.
Not long after, he was summoned by imperial decree to preside over Mount Ling-shan. The number of students seeking instruction there daily did not fall below several thousand.

During a year of famine, when the multitude of wandering monks had nowhere to turn, Mount Ling-shan alone remained open to all; whatever they brought in for their sustenance was always sufficient, and he constructed a monastic hall to provide for them.

He expanded the communal quarters for the assembly and the hall for extensive repentance through diligent cultivation; he increased the number of cultivated fields, ensuring that no expenditures were left unmanaged.

He once composed the "Ten Admonitions for the Abbot" to warn himself against shortcomings, striving for sincerity to perfect his wise conduct, relying on meditative concentration and wisdom to guide his monastic discipline, propagating moral virtue to welcome those yet to come, and honoring Buddhist merit to benefit the national destiny.
He assessed talents and abilities to appoint capable assistants.

He harmonized ritual and righteousness to discern safety and peril; he employed the *siddhāntas* to respond to the various capacities of beings. He practiced frugality for himself to restore a hundred neglected institutions;

he clarified cause and effect to protect the permanent endowment (*śāśvata*). He established laws and measures to revitalize the administrative order. If one lacks even one of these qualities, what benefit is there in a hollow reputation?
When Master Hong Kui of Pingzhai, the Endowed with Clarity, saw this, he inscribed upon it: "This is like polishing an ancient mirror."

This is the Dharma. After a long time, the radiance becomes transparent and penetrating; it seems there is no need for polishing. Do not let various meditations deceive you, O elder practitioner, by saying that they do not require wiping and brushing away.
At that time, Master Jian of Beijian also had words of praise, and he further exhorted himself with four points:
"To kindle the lamp of the inexhaustible, to continue the stream of the soundless, to sit within the realm of non-arising, and to contemplate the Infinite Life. — Byak (柏)

Master Tingyue elucidated its essential meaning through four verses. He once composed commentaries on the divergences and agreements among masters such as Huiyan and Zhiguan, synthesizing them into a single path to instruct his students.
On the sixth day of the second month of the second year of the Chunyou era (the *yi-hai* year), he passed away at Mount Ling.

One day prior to his death in his private quarters, despite his failing strength, he drafted a memorial to the throne and wrote a final parting letter to the court dignitaries. When someone offered him medicine, he looked at them with a stern expression and said:
"The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding; you should know this. Having written this verse by hand, he cast aside his brush and passed away.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the right of Moon-Plum Peak (*Gwageui-bong*), which was posthumously titled "Complete Illumination" (*Wonyo*). He spent fifty-nine summer retreats and lived to the age of seventy-six.
Approximately two hundred people received ordination under him, and those who attained the Dharma included Dongyeok, Myo-jan, Yeong-gyeong, Yu-ik, and Gwang...
Fú, Rújiǎo, Xīngfú, Huáizǒng, Xiānfú, Huáidé, Yǒngníng, Dàobīn, Yǒngfú,
Débīn, Cígǎn, Pǔhuì, and more than ten others.
The Dharma Master Xiayan Hu was a successor of the Dharma Master;
his style name was Wankong. He belonged to the Xiang clan of Dongjia, a family of hereditary official rank. From an early age, he was endowed with wisdom and attended a private school at home.
He advanced twice as fast as his peers; at thirteen, he left home and received ordination under Master Ding at Yuexing Temple in the prefecture.

As soon as he had completed the full precepts, he informed Master Ding, saying, "I vow to study the Tiantai vehicle. He relied extensively upon various masters, using every spare moment and a clean desk to treat even a fraction of time as gold and jade.
Resolute in his great purpose, he did not dally with brush and ink. On cool nights and rainy evenings, he recited the patriarchal teachings aloud, saying: "I, by means of..."

This was a time for the refinement of sound and rhythm. Suddenly, [Ch’oe] was moved and said: "You, a man of ancient wisdom and vast intelligence, possess a mastery of the Dharma-knowledge that is perfectly suited.

While alive you were a person; now deceased, you remain as your writings. How could I dare not exert myself? He returned to retrieve the two masters' (Sugyong and Hyegwan) bequeathed writings, and by immersing himself in them and turning them over repeatedly, he suddenly attained profound understanding.

Looking back at the various doctrines of others, they were like splitting bamboo—easily unraveled. He went to visit Hyoam at Dongyeoksan Mountain, where Hyoam had already entered a state of silent contemplation.
He recognized [the man’s] talent and responded to his inquiries with composure; their exchange was like a lock fitting its key. He immediately appointed him to preside over many scholars.
For a long time, he wandered between the two regions of China (Zhongzhou) and India (Indra). The two masters, Baiting and Guyun, treated him with exceptional honor and respect.

They subsequently invited him to share their seats, exerting themselves particularly in recruiting him, and expressed this in verse. In the spring of the Jichou year of the Shaoding era, an imperial decree was issued regarding rites for averting calamities.

The Emperor summoned the Abbot of Shangzhu Temple to the Southern Water Gate for an audience. Since the Abbot Ting was on leave, the Master, serving as the Seat-Head (Zuoyuan), received the imperial decree to substitute him in his official duties.
The Emperor’s words were full of praise, and he bestowed lavish rewards upon him. The Abbot Ting had long suffered from eye disease and intended to request retirement.

The Master of the Preface offered to take his place, but [Zhao] Lao declined repeatedly until he finally desisted. Chushi Mingzhi was at Chaogao on the coast; while he was there, the people were suffering from famine and disease. He moved his residence to Yanjing.
Lord Jie Qi and Grand Councilor Zhao invited him with the title of "Great Hero" (Daxiong), but he could only just accept. Later, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Yuanjue Temple.

Disciples gathered in endless succession, like thunder rolling and hibernating creatures awakening, each according to their own capacity. Although the profound key had been closed, it was now opened once more. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly, leaving the final sentence incomplete.)
His senior fellow disciples could not fathom him; he first opened the Da-yi-tang (Hall of Great Meaning). There, eminent students raised doubts and posed difficult questions.
When they were stalled by words, he led them toward the flavor and meaning; when they were stuck in the abstruse, he showed them the direct and upright path.
Just as they sought [truth] within that flavor, meaning, and directness, the Milky Way surged and ebbed from his tongue, ensuring that no one remained mired in a single corner of understanding.

Although he had responded to conditions in four places, he had not yet brought forth even a single incense offering. There was an interval, and it was said, "Look within the Nirvana Hall. The assembly could not fathom his intention.
On the day he was to pass away, he finally beat the drum to assemble the multitude. He offered a single incense stick for Xiyuan, to repay his original aspiration.
He wrote a verse, saying: "For sixty-one years, I have played with cleverness until I became clumsy. In my final turn, the void bursts asunder."
He tore his robes, cast away his writing brush, and passed away. His monastic seniority was forty-seven years. His funerary shrine remained for four days;

when cremated, his cranial bone and teeth remained intact amidst the ashes. His stupa was enshrined to the east of Guiyun. The Master was lean and emaciated, yet his intellect was sharp, transcendent, and expansive.

The fish-trap and rabbit-snare are but names and phrases; the bellows and bellows-handle are profound signs. When it was time for exposition, all the volumes were set aside, and he sat cross-legged in silence.
Yet when he took his place at the dais and grasped the fly-whisk, the torrential rush of his eloquence was such that even a breached dyke could not compare to its speed.

Whenever he spoke of the discourse on the Middle Way within the *Three Thousand Worlds*, it was the principle of the perfect endowment of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*). Although this was contained within the subtle sūtras, it was through Zhiyi...

He revealed its secrets; his Dharma-wisdom was grandly expounded, profound, penetrating, and clearly manifest. Jingjue, however, clung to dogmatic attachments and lost the path of gradual cultivation.

Subsequently, he erroneously claimed that the "three thousand [dharmas]" in their essential nature pertain only to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Is this not what is meant by the saying, "a hair's breadth leads to a thousand li"?
In my youth, I took the shortcut through the Zen barrier and entered the boundless chamber of Taibai, where I engaged in a dynamic exchange with various elders.
Consequently, what I observed regarding the principles of exegesis was liberated, elegant, and agile—vastly different from the talk of those who merely carry their scriptures in their bags.
One day, as the lecture reached the passage concerning Kāśyapa dancing upon hearing the lute, Sumeru surging and submerging while rising and falling, and the ocean waters tossing with waves—

Even if the theories of various schools of learning were presented, he would refute them point by point. Waiting until their words were exhausted and their meanings fully spent, he would suddenly point to a pillar and say, "Please explain this for the sake of all of you.
Someone once said to the Master, "Why not compose some written works? The Master replied, "I do not wish to build a house upon a house.
He then explained it further: "Words are used to convey meaning; once the meaning is grasped, the words are forgotten. When words are forgotten, the meaning is revealed."
When even these are forgotten, how can names and forms exist? Nāgārjuna established the school, and Bodhidharma transmitted it separately;

they share the same essence yet differ in their expression. Late in life, Chancellor Zheng An asked: "If one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions all vanish away.
Does 'stubborn emptiness' (wankong) also vanish? The Master replied: "Where do you see stubborn emptiness? He further said: "What a fine Buddha!"

While the hall was not yet furnished with a Buddha image, the Master said, "Where is there that does not honor the Venerable One? Chen Xunqing, the Marquis of Zhao, submitted a memorial on his behalf, and he was granted the title of Great Master Zhenwu.
When other high officials questioned him regarding the Buddhist scriptures, he enlightened them according to their individual capacities, and all were filled with realization.

Clad in a single robe, he lived out his life in dignified seclusion, devoted to filial piety and reverence. When his mother’s illness reached its terminal stage and she was groaning in pain, the Master...

He burned incense and performed repentance with sorrow until he was at peace; nevertheless, at the end of every night, he would invariably wash and rinse his mouth to recite sutras, thereby aiding his parents in the afterlife.

Whether in cold or heat, or in moments of haste, he never faltered. As for his younger brother, he followed conditions without regard for honor or obscurity. He exhausted his alms bowl to establish the temple of Shengxin.
He suspended his own benefit to provide for the poor and those in urgent need; he acted thus wherever he went.
These matters were merely secondary to his primary concerns.

Dharma Master Yongqing, style name Yizhong and sobriquet Guyuan, was a successor in the lineage of Dharma Master Tanguan of Tongzhou. He was born into the Xu family of Haiyan, Jiaxing, during the Jiading era.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the year of Yi-hai, he was able to recite the name of the Buddha while still in his swaddling clothes;
his mother was struck with wonder. At the age of twelve, he followed Master Yi at Guangcheng Wanshou Temple in the district to study the Lotus Sūtra.

Within just three months, he could recite it from memory as fluently as a flowing stream. At twenty, he shaved his head and received full ordination. Morning and night he prostrated before the Buddha. He heard [the teachings of] Yanqing of Huating and Tong...
Master Zhōu’s learning and conduct were superior to those of his contemporaries. Bái Yì went to follow him and mastered his Way after five years.
Later, Bái Yì beheld the Buddha’s radiance at Upper Zhú; Fóguāng Wěi took notice of him and subsequently appointed him as his successor.

In the *Xinhài* year of the Chunyu era, he entered the world at Bào Cí Temple in Chǔshàn. Ten years later, all neglected matters were restored, including the contributions of Qū Gōng Yuè, Cháng Gōng Mào, and Jí Gōng Yòng.

Lei came to know of this through these means. There was one who donated five *qǐng* of fields to establish a lecture hall (*guāntáng*). The district magistrate commissioned a scholar to compose an inscription for it.
In the year of Xīnyǒu, he moved the new images to Xīngfú Temple in Hángzhōu and constructed a lion-throne pavilion (*níxuān*). He lectured on the scriptures without a single day’s interruption.
In his leisure time, he would supplement the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* together with like-minded colleagues; students who had not yet passed the state examinations relied upon him for their studies.

Additional fields were granted to provide him with gruel and porridge, and his reputation spread far and wide. On the *renxu* day, he was summoned to the Inner Sanctuary (*naidaochang*) for repentance and prayer;

his efficacy was proven, and he was conferred the title of Master Xiangying (*xiangying fashi*) and invested with purple robes. In the winter of the *jiazi* year, he was summoned to Funing Palace to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, and his performance met with imperial approval.
Gong Xi-yi of the Inner Hanlin Academy praised his portrait, saying: "He has attained the Buddha-mind. [This was] transmitted.
The Buddha’s mouth [is the source of] blessings; this "Lion's Roar" in the Ningfu Palace is a record of actual events. In the year Jiashu, I returned to my former hermitage.

From that time onward, worldly affairs followed one after another, and I frequently suffered plundering. My imperial edict and *kāṣāya* robe were recovered from the riverbank. I served as the Director of Lectures at Mount Ling for over a year.
Subsequently, under the command of Vice-Minister Yang Gongzhen, I was appointed to reside at Yanfu Temple on Mount Nan Zhu. I once [discussed] with Lin...

[Zhili] publicly discussed the three contemplations in one mind (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*). Lin said, "If one wishes to know the 'emptiness-within-provisionality' of the *Zhìzhě* (the *Zhìyǐ jīng*), it is precisely the 'pervasive totality' of the *Nánhuá* (the *Zhuāngzǐ*).
The Master considered that the doctrine of emptiness and non-being in the *Nánhuá* could not possibly be the same as the true meaning of the three contemplations.
He maintained that these matters cannot be reconciled through words, silence, or written characters. Lin offered this verse in thanks: "Who is able to understand him?"
Samādhi is indeed the great tiger of the ancestral house. He then revitalized the temple, establishing grand regulations;

as elephants, dragons, and clouds gathered in assembly, the ocean of the Teaching flourished greatly from that time forth. To the right of the temple is the site where Dharma Master Zhao preached the sutras, known as the "White Lotus Flower Remains," which still exists.
To the left of the temple is the stupa of the Seng-shi and Seng-tong Ning, situated amidst the weeds.
Mǎng moved east of Zhào and constructed a hall of three bays.
Every eighth day of the month, he gathered forty-eight fellow practitioners to emulate the society of Mount Lúshān and cultivate the *nien-fo* samādhi. One day, he said to the assembly:
"Biàn-cái was at Shàngzhú for seventy years before finally retiring to Lóngjǐng. My age has now reached that point; I cannot remain here any longer. I too shall retire."
White lotuses were vied for by the southern lakes of India; he declined them and did not go there again. While traveling behind the mountains, he planted his monk’s staff and struck forth a spring.
Bubbling up with sweet and delicious water, he cleared it to form a pond, naming it "Auspicious Response" (*Xiángyìng*) to show that he did not forget his origins.
The Master’s appearance was magnificent and refined, and his disposition was pure and open. Wherever he went, he established many works. Although he was old, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* every day.

He remained untiring. There were also sayings and phrases transmitted among his followers. Having personally undergone further hardships and anxieties, he withdrew in single-minded devotion and composed "Songs of a Poor Old Man" to manifest his resolve.
Wearing plain clothes and eating simple vegetables, he followed the natural course of transformation with equanimity.

He subsequently established four or seven-day *Lotus Sūtra* repentance retreats, but managed to perform them only twice. He manifested illness and passed away on the tenth day of the first month of the *xinmao* year. His age was...
Seventy-seven years [of age], fifty-seven years of ordination. At his cremation, his teeth remained unbroken and his *śarīra* were brilliantly radiant.
On the fourth day of the second month, his remains were enshrined to the west of Zhaoning. Mou Yue, a Zhongshundafu, composed an inscription for the stupa, which says: [The inscription follows...]
Formerly, Tian instructed his son, saying: "When I die, you must bury me beside Ximen Bao; he was equal to me in his conduct.

Yet Wang Bo-luan should have been buried near him, for they were alike in spirit across the ages. That Yuan’s stupa is close to Zhaoning—could this not be because their wills and practices were the same?
Master Yetao Mo was a Dharma heir of a Dharma master;
"Fengshan" was his style name. He was a native of Shangyu in Kuaiji.

His father, Chen [name obscured], served as a district magistrate of Leqing in Wenzhou during the Song dynasty and died resisting capture by the Yuan troops. When the Master was in his swaddling clothes, his...
His mother carried him back to their village. Their family became increasingly impoverished. At the age of ten, he relied upon Master De of Dashi Monastery in the prefecture;
there he received instruction in Sanskrit script, and upon seeing it only once, he could recite it from memory. Another five years passed before he shaved his head and received the precepts.

He subsequently followed Master Yitang at Baoben Monastery in Huajing to study the teachings of Zhiyi. When Yitang moved to Guoqing Monastery in Tiantai, he again attended him there, thoroughly investigating all of his [teachings].
Xuexue subsequently traveled to Qiandang and visited Master Yunmeng Ze at Yanfu Temple, where he was appointed to oversee the community.
From this, his reputation rose rapidly. He once transcribed three sets of the Lotus Sūtra by hand; one with ink and two with gold.
Thirdly, he drew blood from his fingers. He was born in Jiqing, Yuyao, during the Shouchi era. Bianxiang eventually returned to Yetai Hall.

During the early Daian era, he traveled to the capital to observe the imperial court. The Kings of Goryeo, Cheng and Zhang, were devoted to the teachings of the Buddha and inclined their hearts toward the Inner Canon.

The Dharma Master was questioned based on the sutras and treatises; his eloquent discourse arose like surging clouds. He was summoned to an audience with Emperor Wuzong, who issued an imperial edict restoring him to the position of Tai-pu-diu.
Having taken charge of the monastery affairs, he extensively undertook construction projects, renovating the halls and chambers as well as the images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and celestial deities.
The following year, he traveled to the capital, where he was granted a golden *naṃśīśa* *kāṣāya* and conferred the title of Fozhi Jia.

He was conferred the title of Great Master (Dashi) with the name Fan Haiyue Baojingmiao. By special imperial decree, he was appointed to lecture on the sutras and was granted the rank of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing) as his foremost honor.
Subsequently, he received an edict from the Crown Prince ordering him to compose the *Biography of the Conduct of the Vajra Dampa Lama*.

Once the work was completed, it was submitted to the Emperor and included in the Tripitaka alongside the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. He was bestowed with abundant rewards and repeatedly graced by imperial edicts.

He ascended to the abbotship of Tiantzhu Lingshan in Hangzhou, where he exerted every effort to revitalize the monastery. Those who violated the monastic rules were expelled, while those who maintained their conduct and practices were promoted.
Many people stood in awe of him, and students from all quarters sought refuge at his feet; the Master [treated them] all...

He was treated with exceptional courtesy. He once remarked, "A beginner's difficulties cannot be compared to those of one who is mature in age and experience" (and so forth). To repeatedly hold the office of lecturer is merely a matter within his own domain.

For a student of the initial stage to leave their father and teacher, and abandon their native village—were it not for a profound sense of devotion to the Way, how could they have reached such a state?
We who occupy the positions of spiritual masters have failed to draw others forward with proper courtesy, causing them to turn back in despair upon seeing the limits of our capacity;

how could this not make us people who sever the seeds of the Buddha? During the Yan-you era, when the Prince of Shen traveled through Jiangxi, he gathered the eminent virtuous monks of various mountains at Mingqing Lusi in the prefecture to inaugurate a period of repentance for the Cintamanicakra Avalokiteśvara.
Upon the completion of the rites, the officials prepared *kaṣāya* (vegetarian) meals.

Regarding the ceremonial arrangements: the King was seated in the central high seat, while the various mountain monks were placed on lower seats. The Dharma Master spoke with bold words before him, saying, "On this day of the *zhai* ceremony, for whom is it being performed?
To examine these rites, it is truly not the intention of a king to treat the Gate of Teaching in such a manner.

He immediately ordered that the King’s seat be removed. The King joyfully complied and invited the mountain monks to take the high seats. Among those who heard this, there was none who did not [rejoice].

The Emperor approved of this. Soon thereafter, he returned to Yuecheng, where he purchased a separate estate to provide for his mother’s meals and rest within. Whether in prosperity or adversity, he never diminished his resolve.
At the beginning of the Zhizhi era, when Emperor Yingzong ascended the throne, he entered the capital for an audience and was commanded by imperial decree to reside once again at Lower Tiantai.

Fragrant incense and imperial couriers followed one another along the roads; there was not a single day that he did not receive gifts. The following year, he again proceeded to the Imperial Capital and stayed in the West Hall of Qingshou Monastery.
Famous officials and high-ranking ministers followed the Master to discuss the Way; outside his door, carriages and horses were constantly as numerous as those at the banks of the Qi River.
Among them were Lord Zhongbin of Li, Zi’ang of Wuxing, Lord Xianyu Boji of Yuyang, and [Dongyang]...
Liu Gongdao and others were all friends of the Master; their exchanges of poetry and prose filled many scrolls.

Because his mother was elderly, the Master desired to return to his hometown to attend to her. Upon reaching Xiapi, he suddenly fell slightly ill. Looking toward his attendants, he said, "In my past studies and practices, I have seldom pursued material gain.
Although I have held the position of abbot, it has been nothing more than the remnants of a neglected legacy; my strength is failing."

Nengxing was able to contemplate and admire the Emperor’s vast blessings, though he had only briefly manifested his future prospects. Now that things have come to this, the circumstances of the time can be understood.
He said, "If you all can offer white gold for my mother, I shall have no regrets in death. Having finished speaking, he wrote a verse and passed away in his boat.
This was the tenth day of the eleventh month of the Bingyin year. His disciples escorted his remains back to be buried at Shou.
He passed away at the Stone-Strange Mountain (Seok-gi-san). His secular age was eighty-five, and his monastic seniority (*saṅnag*) was forty-three.

Among his writings were the *Du-jiao si-ji* (Private Notes on Reading the Teachings) and his poetry and prose, titled the *Tian-you ji* (Collection of Heavenly Wandering), for which the former Quanzhang Academician, Lord Yu of Shu Prefecture, composed a preface.
The Master’s spiritual appearance was majestic and transcendent; his voice resonated like a bell. His brilliant character and resolute spirit shook the mountains and rivers. From the state...
The imperial house held the vehicles of the Dharma in high esteem. Among the masters within the realm, there were none who did not exert their strengths to hasten toward this supreme transformation.

Thus, the worldly path became increasingly orderly and the teachings flourished ever more vibrantly. The Master entered and exited the inner palace for twenty years, serving through three successive reigns.
That sagacious sovereigns and worthy ministers were able to utilize the wondrous teachings of our Buddha to mend the flourishing era and support the foundation of the Dharma,
such that those in the southeast who propagated the Tiantai school responded like jade to golden bells and were held in high esteem by the world— this was surely no mere coincidence.
The Dharma Master Yunze, styled Liweng, was a successor of the late master of Shanyuan.
He styled himself Yunmeng and was a native of Shanxi in Yue. His secular surname was Qiu.
When he was born, his paternal uncle dreamed that a divine being descended from the east, with carriage, robes, and attendants of extraordinary appearance.

The following day, auspicious colors filled the curtains and a wondrous fragrance pervaded the chamber when she gave birth. While still in swaddling clothes, his spirit was serene and abundant; by the age of seven, he resembled a mature adult.
He did not partake of worldly flavors. At fourteen, he left the household life at Baoen Temple, where he received ordination under Dharma Master Miaowu of Shan Yuan.
The following year, he received full precepts. He studied the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, mastering their great meanings.

At that time, Miaowu presided over famous monasteries throughout the regions east and west of Xizhou, with several hundred students constantly attending him. The Master served him with the ritual vessels and robes, acquiring [his teachings] in their entirety.

Regarding his path, the principle of the threefold contemplation within a single mind was perfectly clear and beyond doubt. At the age of twenty-nine, he left [his teacher] to reside at Chongshou Monastery;

like a blade newly honed on a whetstone, those with arrogant pride withdrew from his assembly. He subsequently moved to Guangfu, where he restored what had fallen into ruin and reclaimed encroached lands; the stone inscription commemorating these deeds still stands today.

He ascended again to Yanqing Monastery, where the lecture hall was grandly opened. The towers and halls were newly renovated; the morning gruel and evening drums were harmonized, and the annual income increased.

Because the profound teachings had fallen into decline at Gushan, the Master arose and restored the monastery, so that the seat established by the mountain’s founder could be inherited for generations to come.

Because the Chan school had supplanted the teachings at Guoqing, the Master emerged and settled the doctrinal discourse, so that the dust of the "Rain of Flowers" was transmitted to his fellow disciples. This was the foundation.

He established the origins of the Gongyang Temple, planning its layout and propagating its teachings; he assessed the strategic terrain to expand its blessings, providing instruction and revitalizing the institution.
Reaching down to Yaoyuan and the Five Hundred Arhats Temple, he honored and expanded them while maintaining their discipline.
On Mount Yu, he built Baoen as a place for his retirement, and at Longjing, he founded Anxiang.
He became a refuge for the students of the ten directions. At Ba’en in Shan, he further honored his teacher’s hometown;
in every way, he provided him with grand buildings and granted him land and fields. Thus, his intent to repay the kindness of Ci’en was truly diligent.

On two occasions, the Master visited the imperial court, where Emperor Shizu Shen-gong Wen-wu summoned him for an audience, inquired about the great principles of the Buddha-dharma, and bestowed [honors upon him].
At the Qixiang Hall, he was presented with a large robe of red-gold brocade and bestowed with the title "Buddha-Wisdom Profound Eloquence" (Fohui Xuanbian).
Imperial edicts were repeatedly issued, its radiance spreading throughout all quarters. That the Chan practitioners came to regard his teachings as preeminent was truly due to the Master’s merit.

It would not be an exaggeration to say that Zhang Gongbi, the Hanlin scholar Bichun, was the foremost authority on the teachings of provisional and ultimate truth and a great master of the Complete and Sudden school.
On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the Great Virtue’s *dingyou* year, he left behind a verse and passed away at Yanfu Temple in Southern Zhuzhou.
Eight days later, his disciples enshrined his remains in a stupa at Anxiang on Longjing Hill.
He was sixty-seven years of age and had fifty-three years of monastic seniority. His disciples who received the Dharma were Zhi’an, Yuanjing, Xingcheng, Jingzhen, Zongqu, and others.

There were over forty such individuals. The Master visited renowned monasteries and returned seven times to the Daochang temple. On two occasions he was honored with imperial edicts; thrice his status as a paragon of virtue and conduct was elevated.
His brilliance, like that of a blazing flame, shone so brightly that kings, dukes, and high ministers all came to inquire about the Dharma.
It is no wonder that eminent masters and scholars of the highest caliber bowed their heads in submission and took him as their guide. Indeed, there is a profound reason for this.
Dongping Wufashi’s Dharma heir (under Foguang), Master Yuankai, styled Nansou, was the first seat at Yanfu Temple in South India. He took up residence at Guangfu Temple in Qingzhen.
Originally, the temple faced west and its layout was circuitous; it was proposed that a direct road be opened to rectify this, but for thirty years the project could not be accomplished.
The foundation was thus completed. In the third year of the Yanyou era, once Nan’ou arrived, he made the propagation of the Teaching his urgent priority.

Consequently, those who followed him increased in number day by day. He then built a bridge over Furuangpu (Lotus Pond) called Cui-bo (Emerald Waves). Clearing away the thickets and filth, he reached directly to the carriage-road leading to the tomb.
He constructed a gate and hung upon it a plaque inscribed: "The Patriarchal Barrier of Che-xi. He further erected a pavilion named Jingyuan (Scenic Distance), for the purpose of...
This honors the ancestors; it was here that the true path was first opened and great levelness attained, thereby continuing their will. The Grand Councilor of Song, Mr.
Chen Jianqi, offered sacrifices at this temple and engaged in discourse on the Way and the composition of poetry with the great Confucian scholar Ye Tianjing and the poet-monk Dayuan Sōu Hongzhi.
They built the Sanlao Pavilion (Pavilion of the Three Elders) by the riverbank, which has long since fallen into ruin. Nanʼou likewise established [his residence] upon its foundations.
A pavilion was constructed to restore it to its former state, thereby honoring the worthy. Zhou Renrong, a Hanlin Waitzhi, wrote in the temple record:

"The conduct, learning, and professional achievements of Nansou were far superior to those of the common crowd; his establishment of this site is fitting, as it serves to illuminate the virtues of the sages of antiquity."
Therefore, I joyfully record this for posterity.

The Dharma Master Fashu, a successor of the Dharma Master Fayi, took the character "Deng" from his given name as his monastic title, "Zantang. His family was originally from Kuaiji in Yue. Furthermore...
He took Yuexi as his pen-name. His father was Mr. Sun Man, and his mother was Lady Jiang. She dreamed that a solar disc fell from the sky;

upon waking, the morning sun was shining directly upon her bed, and the Master was thus born. From childhood, he possessed extraordinary qualities. At the age of four, while playing, he took up a brush and drew images of Buddhas.
When given the scriptures and books, he was able to recite them immediately, as if it were the result of past cultivation. In the year of Ziyin of the Zhizhi era (1276),...
He left the household life and entered the Stone Gate (Shimen) Hall of Guofo Temple under Master Shu. The following year, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He took the Lotus Sūtra as his daily recitation. Master Shu remarked, "The Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods has the precepts as its foundation.

[Zhiyuan] thoroughly mastered the meanings of the prohibitions and natures, the dual and single regulations, and the permissions for cessation and action. In the year of Yiyou, he first relied upon Master Xian of Fojian.
Adhering to the teachings of Tiantai, he heard of the flourishing of the lecture halls at Mount Jue and went there once more to rely upon them.
He soon returned to serve at Shimen, where at that time Master Hongdao Fufu and Master Jinggong Rensou were nearby;
both masters were giants of the Chan school, and through daily consultation and inquiry, he gained great benefit. Upon the passing of Shimen, he then visited Master Yunmeng Ze.
In South India, he was immediately recognized and held in high esteem. He successively occupied important official posts.
Mount Tiantai’s Guoqing Temple was the actual place where the Great Master Zhizhe practiced his Way; [the temple] had been seized and its teachings changed to Chan.
The Master traveled several thousand li from afar to the capital and reported the full details of these events to the Xuanzheng Yuan, which subsequently restored the temple to its original state.
Formerly, because the Secret Teachings were not transmitted to the Eastern Lands, he received the precepts from the Master Dampa;
having entered his chamber, he was granted the name Juehai Yuanming. Furthermore, he studied the dharma-gates of cultivation under the Master Hasum and thoroughly investigated their essential tenets.
In the year Yiwu of the Yuanzhen era, he entered the capital for an audience with the Emperor and was granted a meal within the imperial palace.
Furthermore, taking Guoqing Monastery as his concern, the Xuanzheng Yuan petitioned the throne for the issuance of an imperial edict to provide protection.
He was then commanded to have Master Hong take charge of it, so that he might distinguish the authentic lineage, support the foundations of the teaching, and provide a refuge for future generations.
The Master intended to travel east to Goryeo to seek out the lost texts of Tiantai; he first submitted a letter to the reigning king of that country, and the kingdom replied.
Finding no further prospects for his mission, he ceased his travels and returned to the capital. There, he took leave of the Emperor and departed.
In the year of *Dingyou* during the *Dade* era, he entered the world at Xingyuan in East India. In the year of *Dingwei*, the region of Wuyue suffered a great drought;

the Master preached the Dharma and offered prayers for rain, moving the hearts of many well-off families, who pointed out their own resources to provide relief. Those who could not support themselves died, yet there was nothing with which to provide them with coffins.
He then enshrined his remains and held a great assembly to universally deliver them. In the year of Great Earth-Monkey (1308), he moved his residence to Yanfu Temple in South India.
The local governor reported his spiritual conduct and his meritorious deeds in saving people and benefiting all beings to the Xingxuan Yuan;
this was subsequently reported to the imperial court, which issued an imperial edict to grant him special protection. In the year of Zhizhi Water-Dog (1322)...

He was summoned by imperial decree to the capital and presented himself at Mingren Hall. By imperial command, he was assigned to the Qingta Temple to collate the Tripiṭaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

The relevant authorities provided him with accommodations, and the annual gifts and honors bestowed upon him were exceptionally generous. When the Emperor visited Wenshu Pavilion, he was summoned for an audience and received the Emperor’s inquiries and greetings.
He was granted a meal on the first day of the New Year, and again attended the Great Bright Hall (Daming Dian) on the occasion of the Tiānshòu Festival, where he was further honored with gifts.

The collation and correction of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* having been completed, he was specially granted a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* robe along with bolts of imperial clothing and travel warrants for the postal stations.
As he was about to return south, an imperial decree suddenly arrived ordering him to establish a great *shuilu* assembly at Baitasi Monastery.

He was urgently summoned by the Duke of Dongping, Zhongxian Wang, who requested him to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma. The multitude were moved and submitted to his teachings; hearing of this, the Emperor’s favor and rewards toward him became even greater.
The Emperor was deeply impressed and issued an imperial decree to bestow his protection, posthumously conferring upon him the title of Great Dharma Master Fohai.
At that time, all the literary and court officials composed poems to celebrate this honor. In the Jiazi year of the Taiding era, he was selected to reside at Upper Tianzhu;

seven years passed until the Xinwei year of the Zhi-shun era. On the first day of the sixth month of that year, he beat the drum to address the assembly, saying: "This is my third residence at a famous mountain."

More than thirty years have passed; my own practice has been of no benefit, and worldly conditions are limited. Although I am ashamed of my own lack of talent, the noble example of the ancient masters can still be emulated.
He then spoke a verse, comparing himself to a dragon returning to its well because of his eloquence. Despite the community’s earnest efforts to detain him, he would not stay.
Ultimately, he shook out his robes and returned to the clouds beyond the Southern Zhu region. After more than a year, he traveled eastward back to Foguo, where he spent the remainder of his life.

Wherever the Master went, disciples gathered like a surging flood; eminent monks from all quarters who were already renowned for their reputation vied with one another to seek instruction at his feet.
In his instruction, guidance, and encouragement, he never for a moment grew weary. Having completed the lectures on the *Four Books* in both their major and minor versions, he would begin them anew.

His eloquent discourse and vast erudition were as swift as the wind and surging as the tide; those with doubts that remained unresolved were settled by him in just a few words, such that everyone attained a clear and cooling understanding.

In his later years, he dedicated his will to the practice of pure karma (*śuddha-karma*). Whether morning or evening, he maintained constant mindfulness, never ceasing even when ill. Once, while secluded...
Secluding himself from all distractions, he practiced the "Gate of Contemplation" with single-minded focus for seven days and nights, frequently experiencing auspicious responses.
As for managing secular affairs, he was never weary of even the most minute details. Where regulations were deficient or decrepit, he expanded and refined them;
where dwellings were dilapidated, he repaired and completed them; where resources were meager, he provided for them through careful planning. He did not allow these matters to... [be neglected].
He had neglected conditioned things and the fruit of Buddhahood had long been abandoned. The Master retired there to rest, yet he was moved by the gravity of Shimen’s entrustment;
emptying his own purse, he renovated it entirely. One day, as the assembly made their customary inquiries regarding the date of the month, the Master suddenly greeted them, saying:
"Had this old monk not retired from public life, twelve years would have passed with half of my journey already completed. Today..."

One day he was present; the next day he was gone. How can the passage of time be grasped? Having already troubled the great assembly to mark his belongings with their pointing fingers as a token of impermanence, the assembly began to recite the Buddha’s name.
The Master said, "Stop, stop! You must each recite the Buddha’s name for yourselves. The next day, they again took the trouble to see him off.
At dawn the following day, the assembly gathered; he sat upright, wrote a verse, and passed away on the second day of the eighth month of the Renzi year of the Zhizheng era.
He was seventy-eight years old. In the sixty-fourth year of the Xia calendar, his entire remains were interred at Qingtai Monastery.

Previously, while at Upper Zhi, the Master had established the Liuxiang Pagoda Cloister to enshrine the founding masters Dharma-master Zhen and Dharma-master Ru, and he had carved his own likeness to the left of them.
Upon arriving here, he divided his fingernails and hair to construct a pagoda within it, as well as at South Zhi.
He established the Mingjing Pagoda Cloister as a place for later generations to pay their respects.

His writings—including the *Collected Annotations on the Diamond Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Sūtra for the Elimination of Calamities*, the *Phrase-by-Phrase Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra*, and the *Yìrúlùn on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra*—as well as his ritual classifications for incantation sūtras, have all been circulated in the world.
Those who inherited his Dharma include several individuals, such as Hongji, Benwu, Yunruo, Da'an, and Shanji.
Dharma Master Mengrun, a successor of Dharma Master Guyuanqing, was styled Yugang.
He was of the Gu family of Haiyan; his father was Min, a reclusive gentleman, and his mother was of the Qiang family.
She was the niece of the Dharma Master Qinggong of Xiangying. While her mother was pregnant with her, she experienced a miraculous dream.

At the age of fourteen, she left home and took refuge with Qinggong at Bailianhua. She once prostrated before the guardian deity of the monastery (Gāraladeva), whereupon the earthen statue suddenly fell over as if returning the bow.

Those around her were all struck with awe. When given Buddhist scriptures to recite, she could chant them from memory upon hearing them once. She was subsequently instructed by the monk Yixiang of the Ritual Office.

He became a teacher. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he studied such works as the *Golden Scalpel* and the *Ten Non-dual Gates* under Guanyuan, and was immediately able to comprehend their great meaning.
When Guanyuan passed away, he further pursued the completion of his studies under Master Chuan of Zhutang.
Due to his arduous studies, he contracted a strange illness; he then performed the Seven-Seven Day Repentance of Invoking Avalokiteśvara, and having obtained a miraculous response, [he was restored].

His illness was cured and his mind became doubly clear and sharp. He diligently preached and diligently practiced. While serving as the *karmadāna* at Jiqing Monastery, he shared the teaching seat at Yanfu Monastery.
When Master Tanzang Cheng arrived to preside over the teaching seat, it was hailed as a period of extreme prosperity. The Master ascended to the position of the First Seat (*prathamapada*).

In all that he expounded, his words were fluent and his meaning manifest; thus, the elderly and established scholars all held him in reverent admiration. He subsequently emerged from the monastery at Haiyan.
Dezang lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* during the long summer retreat; those who came to listen numbered more than a thousand each day.

Even butchers and wine-sellers changed their vocations for the sake of the Dharma, and auspicious responses were beyond counting. When he moved to preside over Fufeng Monastery, his spiritual influence flourished even further.
After six years, he retired to Bailianhua to cultivate the *nienfo samādhi*, and those who followed him increased in number daily at the lecture hall of Master Zhao.

He preached *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for them, and in the intervals spoke to his disciples, saying: "Is this not what our ancestor Zhiyi meant when he said that 'beyond the wind, smoke, mountains, and waters, one’s feet forget their worries;
within the wondrous wisdom and profound dhyāna, the mind is filled with joy'? From this time forth, I vow never to leave the mountain.
However, the Xuanzheng Yuan forcibly summoned him to Ling Shan at the Lower Zha Temple. At that time, the temple had recently been destroyed, leaving only the Puxian Hall.
The Hall of the Venerable One (Xian-dian) remained standing in its grandeur. He sighed with emotion and said, "This temple was established through the compassionate clouds [of the patriarchs].
Since one hall still remains, the vow-power of the Founding Master (Zu-shi) endures. Thereupon, he first undertook its repair and subsequently constructed the various halls and quarters.

Yet, he did not allow the labor of overseeing the construction or the administrative burdens to cause him to neglect his teaching; day and night he lectured without showing the slightest sign of weariness, leading his fellow practitioners to cultivate themselves.
Through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, he was moved by the manifestation of auspicious signs as Samantabhadra emitted light.

After three years had passed, fearing that his worldly engagements would obstruct his original aspiration, he returned to Bailian to spend his final years. On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested the sign of passing away.
He called his disciples Shi, Faming, Ce, Shizhi, and An, instructing them in the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and further told them: "My life..."
His conditions were nearly exhausted; now was indeed the time. Suddenly, he examined the names of the Buddhas and passed away with serene composure.

His worldly age was sixty-eight, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was fifty-four. On the third day of the first month of the following year, he was cremated. Śarīras were obtained from among the remaining ashes.
Previously, while the Master was still in good health, someone had requested that he be interred in a stūpa beforehand. He declined the request with a verse, saying: "Death..."
Later, after his cremation, his single illusory body was reduced to white bones, which were then burned to dust. What need was there for a stone pagoda to mark his name?
In the end, from the beginning, such a person never existed. Consequently, the man did not dare to request [a pagoda] again.
At this time, the master’s disciples constructed a pagoda at Liúwéitíng in Báiliánhuāyuàn below Fēnghuánglǐng to enshrine his *śarīra*. Regarding his writings:

He particularly could not endure the clamor and entanglements of worldly affairs; whenever he encountered them, he would withdraw to avoid them. Seeing that the administrative duties at Yanqing were increasingly burdensome and complex, he immediately constructed a riverside cottage on the shores of Nanhu Lake to spend his final years there.
In the second year of the Zhizheng era, he was summoned by the High Official of the Shixing Yuan, Li Na-lin, to lead the military forces.
He resided at Upper Tianzhu for three years. In the year Guiwei, he manifested parinirvāṇa; his secular age was fifty-eight and his monastic seniority forty-two.

Zhandang’s face overflowed with joy, saying, "A true successor of the Dharma wheel; I have high hopes for you in the future.

When Master Zhou Wen of the Song dynasty was residing at Jiqing Temple, he admired the Master's learning and invited him to serve as the *qubin* (assistant director). Subsequently, he oversaw the *chan* (confessional) rites. Zhandang again summoned the Master to reside there.

At the end of his tenure, Southern India was long celebrated as a sea of the teachings. The Master’s proclamation of the *zong* (Dharma-lineage) had gained renown, standing preeminent throughout the four quarters.
When Zhantang moved to Upper Mount Tiantai, Yugang Run came to fill his position; however, the Master remained in that office.
Disciples gathered from all sides, and there were none who did not imbibe its richness and drink its essence until they were fully satisfied before departing. The year was Tianli Jisi (1389).
He traveled to Daxiong at Liangzhu, where he lectured daily on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. In a dream, Fazhi said to him, "The sutras you expound accord with my own as two halves of a tally;
it is a pity only that your practice has not yet caught up with your words. Thereupon, he redoubled his diligent application of the path of progress.
In the Renwu year of the Zhizheng era, Gao Gong Nalin became the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Xuanzhengyuan) and moved [the master] to reside there.
At Tianzhu Jianfu Monastery, on the Bingxu day, the Left Vice President of the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration Bureau, Duke Duorji, took charge of the monastery’s affairs.

[The Master] was then promoted to serve as the abbot of Nengren Monastery on Mount Tiantai. He presided over three renowned monasteries in total. Those who held the sutras beneath his wheel were for the most part men of noble talent and distinction.

He elucidated the profound meanings of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuanzan*, and the *Wenju*; the fourfold commentaries were made clear and radiant. Furthermore, he exhorted and encouraged [his disciples].

He said: "My ancestors have stated that the single work on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight) is the raft for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, while the ten vehicles and ten contemplations constitute the very essence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
One must let understanding and practice gallop side by side, and employ both the primary and auxiliary methods together;
only then can one ascend to the stages of the Perfect Teaching and not fail the intent of my ancestors in establishing our lineage. Before long, successive military calamities broke out."

His eminent disciple Iseng requested that the Master return to China with the scriptures. The Master joyfully complied. Furthermore, mindful of the swift passage of impermanence, he diligently cultivated pure karma.
He chanted the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing. One day, he gathered the assembly and said:

"The propagation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs depends upon the proper timing and conditions. Since my conditions no longer accord with the times, where shall my teachings find support? It is time for me to return."
He then requested a brush and wrote a verse, sitting upright until his passing. This was on the twenty-second day of the seventh month in the year of Dingyou.
He was seventy-two years old, having lived sixty-three summers. Upon cremation, his teeth, jaw, and tongue-root remained unburnt, and śarīra relics were found in profusion.
His bones were enshrined in a stupa on the western slope of Lingbi. Those who succeeded him in the Dharma were Lingjiu Huigu and others.
Yanqing Ziming, Chongshou Shimeng, Yanfu Furuji, Nengren Jingyu, and others were his disciples. The Master’s character was expansive and generous, and his conduct was steadfastly pure.
He attained profound mastery in all the texts of the Shanjia (Mount Tiantai) school. Throughout the southeast of the Great River, he was esteemed as a patriarch within the teachings.
He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* on several occasions and presided over numerous periods of repentance rituals.
The manifestations of his spiritual responses were manifold and varied. On one occasion, [Zhizhe] requested that he compose a written work to edify future generations.
The Master said: "Our school is fundamentally beyond words and speech. It is only out of necessity that we employ words, so as to manifest the transmission from master to disciple.

Therefore, after Zhan’an compiled the scriptures, there was nothing more than their successive sealing and handing over to one another. Even those who occasionally refuted heterodoxy and protected the orthodoxy—could they have truly desired [to do so]?"
How discerning! Now that the Great Sūtras and the Great Dharma shine as brightly as the sun and stars, one ought to cultivate them without leisure; what need is there to wait for my words?
Those who hear this shall rejoice and be liberated.
