Dharma Master Yungang Run’s Dharma Heir:
Dharma Master Bicai, courtesy name Dayong. His surname was Qu; he was a native of Linhai in Tai. His father, Zhe, was a scholar of the Classics.

The Master’s father was a Confucian scholar of the *ke-mu* (curriculum-based) tradition; his mother was Zhao, who revered the Buddha with great diligence. One night, she dreamed that a divine monk approached her gate shaking a monk’s staff (*zhisixi*). Upon awakening, the Master was born.
As soon as he was able to speak, he could recite the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) by heart. At seven years of age, he was able to compose verses.
At twelve, hearing that Baoen Temple in Sheng County, Yue Province, was the site where the late Master Xianyuan had lectured, he went there to follow him.
Zhai Gong of the West River left the household life, shaved his head, and received full ordination. At sixteen, he visited Master Zhantang Cheng at Nan Zhu Xuanfu Temple.
Upon their first meeting, the Master recognized him as a vessel of the Dharma and appointed him to oversee the guest quarters. At that time, Master Yugang Run was the head of the assembly;

Zhai Gong then took up the scriptures and entered the master’s room for private instruction, never stepping outside the threshold of his quarters for ten years. Regarding all the texts of the Shanjia school...
Regarding the contemplation of the flavor of the teachings, once he was instructed by a single sutra passage, his mind was liberated and his understanding became harmonious.

Master Yugang sighed and said, "Were it not for the latent seeds of practice from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, how could you have attained this? At that time, among his contemporaries, none such as I could surpass him in continuing the lineage;

his brilliant reputation and noble prestige far exceeded those of his peers. As for resolving the essential tenets of the school and determining the chapters of the teachings, everyone invariably deferred to the Master as preeminent.

He became the abbot. Yǔgāng resided at Dècáng on Dāng hú and invited the Master to share the seat of teaching. In the *jiǎzǐ* year of the Tàidìng era, Yǔgāng resigned, and the Master succeeded him to the abbacy.
In the *rénwǔ* year of the Zhìzhèng era, he moved to Xīngfú in Hángzhōu; the following year, he was promoted to Yǎnfú.
He first constructed the Great Buddha Hall, the Treasure Hall, the Main Gate, and the two corridors, as well as the Míxiǎn Hall and the Ten Thousand Buddhas Treasure Pavilion. Its gold...
The azure halls shone brightly as the sacred images were installed with solemn dignity; the grandeur of this Dharma assembly was preeminent among all monasteries.

The Master devoted himself solely to the task of lecturing and disseminating the teachings, distributing all offerings and donations as soon as they were received. Consequently, his architectural achievements were accomplished without toil.
Having heard of his noble conduct, the Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the title "Great Master Fojian Yuanzhao. [The Emperor] sent envoys from Jiangzhe...

Master Xiangda repeatedly presented incense and offerings to seek the Master’s guidance on the essentials of the Dharma. Among the nobility and eminent scholars of the time, there were none who did not incline their hearts with sincerity and pay their respects.
Nevertheless, the Master was so diligent in his contemplative practice that he never faltered in his routine, whether in the bitter cold or the intense heat.

Suddenly manifesting a slight illness, he immediately closed his door and declined all social affairs, intoning the name of the Buddha with such intensity that his voice did not cease for even a moment. Regarding this—
Tudu said, "In a lifetime, the point of human existence lies in that final stroke. You should not say that spiritual practice yields no results.

My karmic conditions for the Pure Land are mature; I am now about to depart. He then prepared himself with a bath, changed his robes, and wrote a verse of parting for the Chancellor and those who knew him.
Sitting upright with palms joined, he passed away on the nineteenth day of the third month of the Jihai year. The *sha*... [funeral rites followed].

On this day, a thousand people gathered to watch. Although the fire had already consumed his tongue and roots, his teeth were not scorched. His *śarīra* relics were like beans; people vied with one another to collect them.
His disciples erected a stupa at the southern side of the monastery for his enshrinement. He lived to the age of sixty-eight and had spent fifty-six years as a monk (*bhikṣu*).
The Master was a man of dignified gravity who spoke little and seldom smiled; yet when he preached the Dharma for the assembly, his words flowed like pouring rain or a surging river.
His mastery was unhindered across all fields. His writings include the three great works—the *Miaoxuan*, *Wenju*, and *Zhi guan*—along with their supplements, commentaries, and auxiliary texts;
lecture notes on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; and liturgical texts for the three patriarchs of Zhang'an, Jingxi, and Siming.
Among those who received his Dharma were Shangzhu Dashan, Xiazhu Liangyu, Bailian Mingde, Pufu Yuanzhen, and Nengren Jiu-huai.

The Dharma Master’s courtesy name was Tianyan. In his youth, he belonged to the Lu clan of Yunquan in Jiahe. His father was Xiang and his mother was Zhang. She conceived him after experiencing a miraculous dream;
from birth, he was exceptionally distinguished, with eyebrows and eyes like embroidery. Whenever he read a book, he would immediately grasp its essential meaning.
At the age of thirteen, he relied upon Yi Lang of Nengren Temple; at sixteen, he shaved his head under Master Cai of Changde An in that same temple.
The family regulations were strict; he was provided with ritual gifts and sent to study under a renowned master, whereby he was able to compose poetry at an early age.
Both Mr. Chou Renyuan and Mr. Bai Ting marveled at his talent. Later, while residing at Yanshou on East Lake, Master Yugang Run taught him the doctrines and contemplations of the Tiantai school.
It was as if they were his long-standing karmic predispositions. Yugang told him, "In the future, you will surely become a vessel for the Dharma. However—"
"I am old and nearing my end; I cannot complete your legacy. Thereupon, he again followed Master Shou of Songhe to thoroughly investigate the principles of the "One Mind and Three Contemplations.
He instructed Yong and Zongsheng to cultivate the Samādhi of Great Compassion.

During this period, the Master dreamed that he ascended to the summit of a great pagoda inscribed with the words "Nitya-sukha" (Eternal Bliss). Upon awakening, he realized, "This is the realm of all Buddhas. The next day, he read...

Regarding the *Awakening of Faith*: when one reaches the point where there are no longer any mutual perceptions of self and other or of material forms, and only the wisdom of True Suchness (*tathatā*) remains alone, there is a sudden realization.
From that time on, his eloquence and exposition became unimpeded. Yan Fangzhujiju Jian invited him to preside over the monastic registers.

Master Dugong of Yuanjue Yunhai summoned his followers, and wherever he went, he was renowned for his reputation. In the second year of the Zhizheng era, the Xuanzheng Yuan appointed him as the abbot of Guangfu Temple on Mount Chexi.
Thereupon, he established the Lotus Sūtra Repentance (Fahua Chan). To the east of the temple complex, he subsequently cultivated the methods of repentance, making it an annual tradition.
He renovated the Many Treasures Pagoda and the new quarters of the abbot’s residence, restoring what was ruined and repairing what was dilapidated; students gathered there like clouds.
In the seventeenth year [of the reign], Xie returned home and built a hermitage, saying: "I shall spend my final years practicing the Pure Land path, as if dreaming of the Lotus.

The Magistrate of Hujun invited him to preside over Cigan Temple. After residing there for three years, he encountered a year of famine; he begged for alms while gathering disciples, never ceasing his lectures and instruction.
When he moved to Yanfu Temple, only three months had passed when the siege of Taicheng occurred. He fell slightly ill, and someone asked about it.
The Master said, "When the number [of years] reaches this point, who can escape it? He sat cross-legged in meditation and passed away.
His remains stayed in the shrine for three days, his countenance unchanged. During the cremation, his tongue remained like the petal of a blue lotus;

his prayer beads and teeth were like strung pearls, all of which were taken away by people. Those from the five commanderies who served together and people from all quarters were without exception moved with grief.
Alas! The Master once fashioned an image of the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Great Compassionate One and served it. Throughout his life, he constantly prayed, saying:

"May I obtain the benefit of even a single sentence or a single verse of the Great Dharma, and bestow it all upon others. Therefore, he was able to respond to circumstances according to their capacities, always attaining the sublime in his actions.
He presided over thirty-seven assemblies for the *Lotus Sūtra* and *Amitābha* repentance rites. He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* until he had completed three full cycles.
Master Shou ordered the transcription of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in silver characters, which were enshrined within the Hall of the True Dharma (*Zhengfa Lou*).

For several years, he did not eat beyond midday. He delighted in receiving guests, regardless of whether he had sufficient resources. When faced with hardship and peril, he remained composed and serene.
After his passing, the monk Daoli interred his remains on the banks of the New Creek. He was sixty years of age; he had been a monk for forty-five years. His dharma heir was Dingjue.

Master Churen, whose formal name was Songhe, belonged to the secular surname Xu. He was a native of Wucheng in Xizhou. His father was Yingyan, a family that had transmitted the Confucian tradition for generations.
From his youth, the Master grew weary of dwelling in the mundane world and left the household life at Yanfu Monastery in Nanzhu, following Master Liutang Quan.
Master Gong attained ordination. He recited the sutras and paid homage to the Buddha day and night without ceasing; he did not eat past midday, and his side never touched his mat.
He strictly maintained the prohibitive precepts, becoming increasingly steadfast as time passed. In the *Xinyou* year of the Zhizhi era, Master Run of Yugang came to reside on this mountain.

Upon hearing of his wondrous teachings, he immediately established himself in wondrous practice. His reputation for the Way spread month by month, and he eventually ascended the high seat to serve as a teacher to scholars and the assembly.

He instructed several hundred people, revealing the teachings according to their capacities without ever showing the slightest weariness. Monastics and laypeople throughout the rivers and lakes vied to have him emerge from seclusion to head a monastery.
His mother was virtuous and discerning; she would often admonish him, saying, "Be careful not to take up residence in a temple and trouble me.

He strictly followed his mother’s instruction; whenever those came with marriage proposals and gifts, he spoke to them with stern refusal and would not accept them, while regarding his own spiritual practice—
Her merit increased as she redoubled her diligence. She practiced the four samādhis, completing them and then beginning them again.
Whenever anyone offered her wealth or goods, she would immediately distribute them equally among the assembly. With what she herself obtained, she ransomed birds and fish to set them free.

In the year Jiazi of the Tai Ding era, she established the Zhenru Guantang (Hall for Contemplating True Suchness) to the north of Hangzhou City; her mother donated all the contents of her dowry to provide for the expenses of the construction. The hall...

He successfully completed the consecration and enshrinement of a thousand-headed Avalokiteśvara image. Every year, during the month of the late autumn, he would assemble his fellow practitioners to perform the Great Compassion Repentance for twenty-one days.
He established a separate Puṇyākara (Samantabhadra) ritual arena and annually practiced the Lotus Samādhi.
He constructed a multi-storied pavilion, placing a Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra written in gold and a Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra written in silver upon its upper level, while opening up the space below.
It was used as a lecture hall. Whenever the Master preached the Dharma, he often moved the heavenly deities to attend his seat, and the heavens rained down precious flowers.
On the second day of the second month in the second year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested illness and addressed the assembly, saying: "One day before the Buddha entered nirvana, I shall depart.
Build a Pure Land retreat for me to assist my journey to the West. On the thirteenth day, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright until dawn. Broadly...

He preached the Dharma-gate of contemplating the mind and contemplating the Buddha’s Pure Land to exhort his disciples, after which he passed away peacefully at the age of fifty-three, having spent thirty-five years as a monk.
On the day of his cremation, golden light radiated from the center of the fire-wheel;

among the remaining ashes, his tongue remained unburnt, and countless śarīra relics were found. His stupa was erected to the right of the Contemplation Hall. Those who inherited his Dharma lineage were De and Yu.
The Dharma Master Simha’s actual name was Yin Hai; his style name was Xiang-an. He was surnamed Zhong and was a native of Aoxi in Jiaxing.

His mother conceived him after experiencing a wondrous dream. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order under Master Le of Zhiyuan Temple in Haiyan.
He grew weary of and abandoned yoga, devoting himself exclusively to the recitation of Confucian classics. At nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

Hearing that Yugang was preaching the Dharma at Yanshou, he went there to inquire about the essentials of the teachings. Yugang retained him, bestowed upon him various Tiantai texts, and instructed him to master them through diligent recitation.

When Yugō moved to Enpuku-ji, he invited the Master to take charge of monastic affairs. He once practiced the seven-week *kwan-on* (Avalokiteśvara) retreat, during which he had a dream-vision of the Bodhisattva cutting open his own abdomen and extracting his heart;
from this, his intellect became exceptionally sharp. Later, while residing at Byakurenge-in, he received the transmission of *shikan* (calm abiding and insight).
Continuing with the *Miaoxuan* (Excellence of the Profound), his eloquence was vast and unrestrained. When Yugang succeeded him at Zhuzhu Lingshan, the Master followed him there as well.

When Master Dayong Cai moved to Yanfu Temple, he invited the Master to occupy the head seat. Later, he returned to Qiyuan to establish a Hall of Repentance, where he initiated the annual period of repentance;
shortly thereafter, he experienced auspicious spiritual responses. The Magistrate of Jiaxing requested that he reside at Decang in Danghu. This was the third year of the Hongwu era.
By imperial decree, eminent monks from throughout the empire were summoned to the capital to present their views before the throne. [The Master] subsequently returned to Fuyan on Aoxi.
In the eleventh year, an edict was issued for monks throughout the realm to lecture on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Hṛdaya-sūtra*.

The Master expounded upon these teachings at Tianning Monastery in Haiyan, providing great benefit and edification. In the fifteenth year, when Zhu Yin Daogong ascended to Upper Tianzhu Monastery, he invited the Master to reside there.
Regarding his office as *Dujiang* (Chief Lecturer), the following year the Office of Monastic Records selected him to reside at Xiazhu.

For seven consecutive years, he expounded upon various sections of the scriptures in an unceasing, continuous stream. He then retired to Aoxi for only one year, after which he traveled extensively to visit former neighbors and old friends before settling at Dezang.
Suddenly, one day, he composed a verse titled "Meditating on the Pure Land" (*Huai Jingtu Ci*) while sitting upright and reciting the Buddha’s name.
He passed away on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month in the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era, the Xinwei year.

He was seventy-eight years of age, fifty-nine years by the summer reckoning. His disciples enshrined the *śarīra* relics in a stupa on the southern slope of Feilai Peak. Throughout his life, the Master maintained the precepts with great rigor;
in movement or stillness, speech or silence, he never deviated from their teachings. He devoted himself to the diligent study and mastery of the various sections of the Tiantai school.
He pursued his studies until he had reached the ultimate subtlety before ceasing. Whenever scholars came to him with questions, he would tirelessly explain their essential meaning to them.
Wherever he went, the assembly of listeners gathered like clouds; thus, he was able to support and establish the Way of the Teachings, becoming the preeminent authority of his time.

His extant works include the *Brief Commentary on the Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, the *Textual Exegesis of the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, the *Guide to the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Lamp Treatise on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra*, and the *Commentary on the Bequeathed Teachings*.
He also authored the *Notes on the Four-Part Vinaya Precepts*, the *Essential Guide to the Correct Exposition of the Ritual for the Four Teachings*, and the *Inscription on the Golden Scalpel*.
Regarding his practice, he performed seventeen assemblies of the Lotus Period Repentance and two assemblies of the Golden Light Period Repentance.
Thirteen [people] attained auspicious responses: five who aspired to the Pure Land of Amitābha, five who invited Avalokiteśvara, three for Great Compassion, and two for the Constant Sitting Samādhi.
Those who attained the Dharma were Faxi, Daofu, Renrang, Yiqi, Ruizhi, and Miaojie.
The Dharma Master’s name was Dayou, with the courtesy name Qizong. His alternative style was Youqu’an. He was born into the Wu clan of Wuxian County in Gusu.
Both his parents observed the vegetarian fast and were regarded by their neighbors as virtuous people. His mother dreamed of a monk who called himself Śāna; upon waking, she became pregnant.
When he first began to speak, he heard his elder brother reciting the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* and immediately repeated it after him.
At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk under Master Wei-si Gui, shaving his head and receiving full ordination.
Whenever he glanced at any internal or external scripture, he immediately mastered its meaning. Initially, he studied the teachings of Xianshou with Guting as a companion;
subsequently, he followed Master Gaosheng to study Tiantai *zhiguan*. Later, he served within the assembly of Hongjiao and Tianquan Zehui.

Regarding the office of *Chanshou* (Confessional Leader): One day, while reading the *Yugang Sijiaoyi Jizhu* (The Collected Annotations on the Ritual for the Four Teachings by Yugang), he reached the commentary on the first of the five grades, the "Grade of Initial Joy," which states:
"One emptiness is all emptiness; the three contemplations fully manifest the function of destroying appearances. One provisionality is all provisionality;
the three contemplations fully manifest the merit of establishing dharmas. One centrality is all centrality; the three contemplations are entirely... [the text continues].

Upon suddenly attaining a realization of the absolute, independent essence, he thereafter mastered the fundamental frameworks and various treatises of the Tiantai school as if they were long-accustomed studies.
He emerged into the world at Bailian (White Lotus) in Fuli. Subsequently, he received distant instruction from Yugang.

In the fourth year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to the capital as a eminent monk. The following year, he participated in the Great Memorial Dharma Assembly at Jiangshan. In the tenth year of the Hongwu era...

He ascended to serve as the abbot of Beomsan-sa in the north of the prefecture. He lectured on the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, elucidating their profound meanings;

the many scholars followed him with delight. Donors gathered in great numbers, and he consequently constructed a magnificent Great Buddha Hall. Once it was completed, he intended to retire in seclusion and return to his mountain retreat.
At that time, the venerable monks of Jiaxing manifested no concealment and requested the Master to open the mountain at Yuan Tong in the district; it is now the foremost among lecture monasteries.

Not long after, he returned to the Western Hills to build a residence, which he inscribed with the name "Zhenru. There he practiced the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance (nienfo sanmei) without ever ceasing for even a moment.

In the twenty-sixth year of the Hongwu era, a vacancy occurred in the Office of the Buddhist Registry (Senglusi), and he was summoned to the capital. Upon his audience with the Emperor, the Emperor was pleased.

He sighed with regret and remained for over a month. He was appointed as Right Supervisor (You Shanshi) of the Office of Monastic Records (Senglusi). In the twenty-ninth year, he was promoted to Left Supervisor (Zuo Shanshi).
His various compositions written in response to imperial decrees while serving in office still exist. That year, he conducted examinations for the monastics throughout the empire;

his achievements in supporting and upholding the Sangha were preeminent. The Emperor graciously bestowed upon him a *kāṣāya*, robes, bedding, shoes, and varying amounts of paper currency. In the thirty-second year...

He retired from public service to return to his ancestral estate in Gusu. In the summer of the third year of the Yongle era, he was summoned once more to the capital. By imperial decree, he was tasked with compiling Buddhist scriptures;
the Master took charge of synthesizing the essential meanings of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. When the draft was completed, he suddenly claimed to be slightly ill.

On the second day of the first month of the spring in the fifth year, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. He was seventy-four years of age and had been a monk for sixty-two years. On the tenth day of this month...
On the eighth day, at the time of his cremation, auspicious clouds of five colors filled the sky and celestial flowers rained down from above; cranes circled in flight over the pyre.

After the fire was extinguished, countless *śarīra* relics were recovered. Among his works are the annotated commentary on the *Nettippakaraṇa* (The Guide to the Pure Land), the collated editions of the two sutras—the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the lineage chart of the Tiantai school’s oral transmissions, and the *Fahua cuoyao tu* (Illustrated Summary of the Lotus Sūtra) along with the two treatises on the practice and realization of the Pure Land.
Illustrations for the Ritual Text of True Suchness in the Pure Land (*Jingtu zhenru liewen*) in one fascicle; the *Huayan dengke* (Avataṃsaka Lamp Rite) in one fascicle;
and the *Jingtu jiulian dengke* (Pure Land Nine Lotus Flower Lamp Rite) in one fascicle. Compiled by the dharma-disciples Huiche and Dewan.
The Dharma-heir of Master Ziting was the Dharma Master named Huiri, whose style name was Dongming.
He was a native of Chigeng on Mount Tiantai and a descendant of the late Prime Minister of the Song Dynasty, the Duke of Wei, Jia Sidao.
Aspiring to the Gate of Emptiness, he went to Guangyan Temple in his county and took refuge under Master Pingshan et al., shaving his head to become a monk.
At that time, Ziting was lecturing on the teachings of the Tiantai school at Chicheng; [Fazhi] hurried to the base of his wheel to receive those expositions.

Relying on the master’s guidance through the scriptural categories, he was able to grasp their meaning. One day, while taking a nap, he saw bamboo stretching across the ground, with something coalescing upon the bamboo.
There was a bowl of white congee, shining brightly. The Master lay down and ate it. Upon waking, he spoke of it to Ziting.

Ziting said, "The word for bamboo (*zhú*) and the name of the country *Zhú* (India) share the same pronunciation. You have been able to eat on the spot; surely the karmic conditions for this lie between the two instances of 'Zhú'—the upper and the lower.
You should go quickly. He then took up his bottle and staff, crossed the Zhejiang River, and paid homage at the Bamboo Hut to Master Jinggong.
At Upper Zhushan, he was suddenly detained. His quarters were quite damp and low-lying, so the Master composed a poem to describe the situation.
When Zhuwu saw it, he said to the assembly, "This man is no ordinary person; in the future, he shall succeed to the leadership of this mountain. One must not underestimate him because of his youth.
He moved him to a dry and firm location and treated him like a guest or friend. Later, there happened to be construction work to be undertaken.

Those who offered gold and silk arrived in great numbers, crowding one another. When the long-serving monks wished to record the names of the donors, they searched for a skilled calligrapher but could find none to respond to the request.
The Master raised his sleeves and stepped forward, saying, "I shall try to do it. His brushstrokes were like spreading mists and unfolding clouds, their brilliance radiant and vivid.
Zhuyu said, "My previous words were not mistaken. He was then appointed to oversee guests and subsequently took charge of the monastic registers. Zhuyu—
After Wuyi entered nirvana, Zantang came from Yanfu Temple to succeed him on the seat. The Master was invited to reside in the Rear Hall as the head of the assembly.
Before long, he went forth into the world at Wushan. Later, when he was at Shengshui, Zantang missed him and could not bear to let him go;
he summoned him back to the mountain to serve as the First Seat, so as to set an example for the fourfold assembly. Those who came to study under him numbered in the thousands. The Master—
He guided and cleared them according to the depth and shallowness of their natural conduits.

In the fourth year of the Zhongji era of the Yuan dynasty, the Xuanzheng Yuan selected various men of esteemed reputation, and the Master once again resided at Jianfu Temple for three years, through both winter and summer.
